# newsetup

Scaffold projects from **templates**. A template bundles always-on root files
(`config/`) plus any number of optional **modules** (each its own folder), where
a module can run shell commands (e.g. `create-next-app`, `django-admin
startproject`) and/or drop in files.

```
newsetup list                                                    # show templates + their modules + parts
newsetup new --path . --template default                         # all modules + config here
newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend  # one module (+ config) into ./myapp
newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend backend
newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra            # all infra parts
newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra --only rds # just the RDS part (+ its deps)
newsetup new --path . --template default --bare                  # config root files only, no modules
newsetup new --path . --template default --bare --force          # overwrite existing root files (no prompt)
```

## Model

- **`--template`** is required — you always state what you're scaffolding. See
  `newsetup list` for available names.
- **`--path`** is required — no implicit current-directory default. Use `.` for
  here, a name for `./<name>`, or a full path. The folder is created if missing.
- **`config/`** = always-on. Everything in a template's `config/` folder is
  copied to the project **root** on every scaffold (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`). It is not
  a selectable module.
- **Modules** = every other folder in the template (and/or every section in
  `template.toml`). Drop a new folder like `infra/` into a template and it
  becomes a module automatically — it shows in `list` and is selectable with
  `--only infra`. No code change needed.
- **`--modules A B`** builds exactly modules A and B; config still rides along.
  Omit `--modules` to build all modules.
- **`--only x y`** selects **parts within a single module** — legal only when
  exactly one module is selected (via `--modules`) and that module declares
  `parts` in `template.toml`. For example `--modules infra --only rds` builds
  just the RDS part. Parts auto-pull their dependencies (selecting `ecs` also
  pulls `ecr`, `rds`), and each part ships its own `*.tf`, variables, outputs,
  and a `terraform.tfvars.example` fragment that is concatenated into one root
  example. A module can also declare `always` parts (e.g. infra's `iam`) that
  are copied on every scaffold regardless of `--only`. Omit `--only` to build
  all of a module's selectable parts.
- **`--bare`** builds config root files only (no modules). `--bare` cannot be
  combined with `--modules` or `--only`.
- **Config conflicts.** If a root config file (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`) already exists,
  `newsetup` prompts per file: **[o]verride** (replace), **[m]erge** (keep the
  existing file, append a blank line, then the template's content), or
  **[s]kip** (leave it untouched). In a non-interactive shell it aborts instead
  of prompting — pass `--force` there.
- **`--force`** overwrites existing root config files without prompting. Module
  folders that already exist and are non-empty always abort (never clobbered).
- `git init` runs on every scaffold. If any command exits nonzero, `newsetup`
  stops.

### Requires on PATH

`git`, plus whatever a selected module's commands call — `npx` (Node) for
`frontend`, `django-admin` for `backend`. These run as subprocesses via your
system PATH; `newsetup` does not install them.

## Templates

```
new_setup/templates/<name>/
├── template.toml     # description + per-module { cwd, commands }
├── config/           # → copied to project ROOT (always)
│   ├── CLAUDE.md
│   └── README.md     # empty stub
├── backend/          # module "backend": files overlaid into ./backend/
│   ├── .gitignore
│   ├── CLAUDE.md
│   ├── Dockerfile
│   ├── entrypoint.sh
│   └── migration/{seed,backfill}/   # empty (.gitkeep) seed/backfill dirs
├── frontend/         # (optional) overlay files for ./frontend/
├── data/             # module "data": empty folder (.gitkeep)
├── legacy/           # module "legacy": empty folder (.gitkeep)
└── infra/            # module "infra": Terraform, split into PARTS
    ├── _core/        #   always copied: main.tf (provider), variables.tf, .gitignore, tfvars fragment
    ├── iam/          #   always copied: general roles (GitHub OIDC provider + deploy role) — inert until a part grants it
    ├── ecr/          #   part "ecr":  ecr.tf + deploy_policy.tf (push grant) + outputs
    ├── rds/          #   part "rds":  database.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
    ├── s3/           #   part "s3":   storage.tf + outputs
    └── ecs/          #   part "ecs":  ecs.tf + iam.tf (execution/infra roles) + deploy_policy.tf (redeploy grant) + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
```

`data` and `legacy` are pure file-copy modules that ship an empty folder (a
`.gitkeep` so the directory survives in git) — placeholders you fill in per
project. `backend` runs `django-admin startproject` and then overlays its
Docker + `migration/` scaffold on top.

`infra` is a **part-aware** module: instead of one flat folder it has `_core/`
plus `iam/` (both **always copied**) plus one subfolder per selectable part.
`--only <parts>` copies `_core` + `iam` + the selected parts (and their
dependencies) flat into `./infra/`, and every copied folder's
`*.tfvars.fragment` is concatenated into a single
`./infra/terraform.tfvars.example`. Terraform auto-merges all `*.tf` in the
folder, so a part only ever contributes the variables/outputs for resources it
actually creates. Parts declare dependencies in `template.toml` (`ecs` →
`ecr, rds`).

**IAM is split by what a role *is*.** General roles that do nothing until a
policy is attached (the GitHub Actions deploy role + its OIDC provider) live in
the always-on `iam/` layer — declared once, inert by default. Each resource part
then ships the *permission* that lights that role up for itself: `ecr/` grants
image push, `ecs/` grants service redeploy; `s3`/`rds` grant nothing (CI never
touches them). Roles that are inseparable from their policy and meaningless
without their resource (the ECS task-execution + Express infrastructure roles)
live inside the part itself (`ecs/iam.tf`). The role's *trust* policy ("who may
assume it") always rides with the role; only *permission* policies move out to
the parts.

`template.toml`:

```toml
description = "Next.js frontend + Django backend + AWS infra (Terraform)"

[frontend]
cwd = "."                                              # run at root; the command makes ./frontend
commands = ["npx create-next-app@latest frontend --yes"]

[backend]
cwd = "backend"                                        # newsetup makes ./backend, runs the command inside
commands = ["django-admin startproject config ."]

[infra]                                                # part-aware module (no commands)
parts  = ["ecr", "rds", "s3", "ecs"]                   # selectable with --only
always = ["iam"]                                       # copied every scaffold, like _core; not selectable

[infra.requires]                                       # auto-pulled deps when a part is selected
ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]
```

- A module's `commands` run in `cwd` (relative to the project root; default
  `"."`). `newsetup` creates `cwd` first if it isn't `"."`.
- A module's folder contents (if any) are copied into `./<module>/` after its
  commands run.
- A module with no `template.toml` section is pure file-copy (no commands).
- A module that declares `parts` is part-aware: it copies `_core/` + any
  `always` subfolders + the selected part subfolders (flat), resolves
  `requires`, and assembles its `terraform.tfvars.example` from the copied
  folders' `*.tfvars.fragment` files. Part-aware modules ignore `cwd`/`commands`.

Templates ship inside the package and are read at runtime via the installed
package's own files — no dependency on this source folder's location.

**Add a template:** create a new folder under `new_setup/templates/`, then
reinstall.

## Install

Installed as a **uv tool** — uv builds it into an isolated environment and puts a
`newsetup` shim on your PATH (`~/.local/bin`). Snapshot install: code + templates
are copied into uv's data dir, so you can move/rename/delete this folder
afterward without breaking the command.

```sh
# from clis/new_setup/
uv tool install .
```

If `newsetup` isn't found, ensure uv's bin dir is on PATH:

```sh
uv tool update-shell   # then restart the shell
```

## Update

Snapshot install — edits here (code or templates) don't affect the installed
command until you reinstall:

```sh
# from clis/new_setup/, after editing
uv tool install --reinstall .
```

## Uninstall

```sh
uv tool uninstall newsetup
```

## MISSING

Known gaps not yet shipped. The planned `infra` module will ship the RDS box
with financexpo's permissive networking default (`publicly_accessible = true`,
open to `0.0.0.0/0`). That still needs hardening before it's a safe default:

6. The security question — this is the important one

> "I thought without the password it was impossible to access these?"

A password is authentication, not network reachability — they're different
layers, and the financexpo config gets the network layer wrong:

```hcl
publicly_accessible = true
cidr_blocks         = ["0.0.0.0/0"]   # port 5432 open to the entire internet
```

That puts Postgres on the public internet. The password only kicks in after an
attacker has already reached the door and is knocking. So you're exposed to
everything that happens before auth:

- Credential brute-force / spray — bots scan 0.0.0.0/0:5432 constantly; a weak
  or leaked password is then an instant breach.
- Pre-auth CVEs — any Postgres vulnerability reachable before login (they exist)
  hits you directly.
- Info leak — the server advertises its version/existence to the whole internet.

Think "a locked door on a public sidewalk" vs "a locked door inside a gated
building." Same lock; very different risk.

The simple standard: keep the database off the public internet. The app reaches
it privately; nothing on the internet can even open a socket to it. Concretely,
the template default becomes:

```hcl
publicly_accessible = false
# ingress: only the app's security group can reach Postgres — not the world
ingress {
  from_port       = 5432
  to_port         = 5432
  protocol        = "tcp"
  security_groups = [aws_security_group.app.id]   # was: cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
}
```

(If ecs isn't selected, there's no app SG, so it falls back to
var.db_allowed_cidr defaulting to the VPC CIDR — still private, never 0.0.0.0/0.)

And I'll keep a warning comment showing the escape hatch for when you genuinely
need to connect from your laptop — scope it to your IP, never the world:

```hcl
# To connect from your machine temporarily, add an ingress rule for YOUR ip only:
#   cidr_blocks = ["<your-ip>/32"]   # never 0.0.0.0/0
# Better: reach it through SSM port-forwarding / a bastion and keep this false.
```

Strong db_password still required — that's defense-in-depth on top, not instead
of. Net effect: secure-by-default, but you can still get in when you need to.

Now I can explain it concretely against what's actually in the files.

## How it works *right now*

Look at `ecs/ecs.tf` line 21 — this is the whole story:

```hcl
environment {
  name  = "PROD_DATABASE_URL"
  value = "postgres://${var.db_username}:${var.db_password}@${aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint}/...?sslmode=require"
                                                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
}
```

That `aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint` is a **live resource reference** — ecs is reaching directly into the rds part and reading an attribute off the actual database resource. This is the "direct reference / auto-wires in one apply" model.

Consequences of this being how it is today:

- **ecs literally cannot stand alone.** If you `--only ecs`, Terraform sees `aws_db_instance.postgres` referenced but never declared → `terraform validate` fails with a dangling reference. That's *exactly why* `template.toml` has `ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]` in `[infra.requires]` — selecting ecs is forced to drag rds in, because the code won't even parse otherwise.
- **The upside:** when both are present, it's magic. One `terraform apply` creates the RDS box, Terraform notices ecs depends on `aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint`, builds rds *first*, then injects the real endpoint into the ECS env var automatically. Zero manual steps. The DB URL is always correct because it's computed from the live resource.

So today: **ecs and rds are welded together.** "ecs" really means "ecs+rds, always."

## What "the wiring is a variable" means

The decoupled alternative replaces that live reference with a plain input variable:

```hcl
# instead of referencing aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint:
value = var.database_url   # a string you pass in, default ""
```

Now ecs no longer mentions any rds resource. It just wants *a string*. Where that string comes from is none of ecs's business — could be RDS, Supabase, Neon, anything.

"The wiring is a variable, not a live resource reference" = **the connection between the two parts is now a value you type in, instead of a link Terraform follows automatically.**

That buys independence but costs you the auto-magic. Compare the two worlds when you want **both** ecs and rds:

| | Live reference (today) | Variable (decoupled) |
|---|---|---|
| `--only ecs` alone | ❌ won't validate | ✅ runs, no DB |
| ecs + rds together | one `apply`, auto-wired | **two-step apply** |

The "two-step apply" is the honest tax. Because `var.database_url` needs a value *before* apply, but the real endpoint doesn't exist *until* rds is applied, you can't do it in one shot:

1. `terraform apply` → rds comes up. Read its endpoint: `terraform output -raw rds_endpoint` (that output already exists in `rds/outputs_rds.tf`).
2. Paste it into `database_url` in your tfvars, `terraform apply` again → ecs picks it up.

With the live reference, Terraform's dependency graph does that ordering for you in a single apply. With a variable, *you* are the dependency graph.

## The trade-off in one sentence

- **Live reference** = one-apply convenience, but ecs is permanently chained to rds (no "ecs alone").
- **Variable** = ecs works with any database (the actual meaning of "generalist"), but combining ecs+rds becomes a manual two-step.

For a generalist template the variable wins, because the template's job is to scaffold *any* project, not to assume every project pairs ECS with an RDS box in the same stack. The convenience you lose is recoverable any time — a project that's *always* ecs+rds can drop the one-line live reference back in.

One more consequence worth flagging, since it reverses something said earlier: decoupling flips the dependency direction. Today `ecs → rds` (ecs needs rds to exist). Decoupled, ecs needs *nothing* — so `[infra.requires]` would lose the `ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]` rds entry (ecr stays, since the image reference `aws_ecr_repository.backend` is still a live reference). ecs would then pull only ecr.

content.text:
Let me challenge the premise directly, because I think the framing is slightly off in a way that dissolves the problem.

## First: who actually needs that env? Not ECS. Not RDS. The *app*.

`PROD_DATABASE_URL` isn't there because ECS needs it or because AWS requires it. ECS doesn't care — it'll run a container with zero env vars all day. RDS doesn't care either; it just sits there listening on 5432.

That env exists because **Django needs to know where its database is.** It's application config. ECS is just the delivery truck that hands the app its environment at boot.

That reframe matters, because it tells you who *owns* the env: the application — and the application is what ecs deploys. So the DB url conceptually belongs **with ecs**, not with rds. rds isn't the owner of that wiring; rds is merely one possible *supplier of the value*.

## Why your grant analogy inverts here

You're pattern-matching to the IAM refactor we just did: "the grant lives in the part, lighting up the shared thing." That worked for IAM for a specific reason — and that reason is exactly what's missing here.

- **IAM grant (ecr → role):** ecr genuinely *owns* the permission. "I am the ECR repo, and I permit pushes to me." The grant is a fact about ecr. It belongs in ecr/. The role is the shared surface; ecr lights it up. Ownership flows **part → shared thing**. ✅
- **DB env (rds → ecs):** rds does *not* own "the app should connect to me." The app owns its need for a database; rds just happens to be able to answer it. Ownership flows the **opposite way** — the consumer (ecs/app) owns the need, rds is a value source.

So "rds contributes the env to ecs, like a grant" is upside-down. It'd be rds reaching into the app's config to declare what the app needs — rds doesn't have that authority or knowledge. The app does.

## And even if you wanted to, Terraform won't let you

Here's the mechanical wall, and it's the real reason the grant pattern can't transfer:

The IAM grant works because `aws_iam_role_policy` is a **separate, independently-addressable resource**. ecr can put it in its own file; flat-copy merges it; it attaches to the role by reference. Separable.

The DB env is a **nested block inside the one `aws_ecs_express_gateway_service` resource**. It is not separable. And Terraform forbids splitting a single resource across files. So rds *cannot* drop a file that injects an `environment { ... }` into a resource declared in ecs/ecs.tf. There's no syntax for it.

You might think "ok, make the env a `dynamic` block over a variable/local, and have rds fill it." That hits two more walls, both fatal:

1. **The value is computed.** The RDS endpoint (`xyz.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com`) is assigned *by AWS at apply time* — that random hash isn't knowable beforehand. To move a computed attribute from resource A into resource B **in one apply**, Terraform *must* see a live reference A→B in its graph. There is no other mechanism. And a live reference is precisely what makes ecs fail to validate when rds is absent. Computed value ⇒ live reference ⇒ dangles without rds. Unavoidable.

2. **You can't stub-and-override across merged files.** For optional injection you'd want ecs to ship a `local.db_env = {}` default that rds overrides when present. Terraform rejects duplicate local keys — no overrides. And if only rds defines the local, ecs's reference to it dangles when rds is absent. Either way, dead.

So: **at the flat-file-merge level, "rds optionally injects the DB env into ecs" is not buildable.** Not "hard" — structurally impossible, because computed-value-coupling forces a live reference and Terraform offers no override/stub escape. There is no clever HCL that gets you there.

## The only two real escapes (and they're big)

**Escape A — runtime indirection (the *true* grant analog).** Stop putting the URL as a literal env. Instead, ecs's task references a secret by a *conventional name* — a string like `/${project}/${environment}/DATABASE_URL` (SSM Parameter Store / Secrets Manager). A string isn't a Terraform reference, so ecs validates alone. Then rds contributes a **separable** `aws_ssm_parameter` resource (lives in rds/, exactly like ecr's deploy_policy.tf lives in ecr/) that fills that name with the computed endpoint. One apply, no dangling ref, ecs standalone-valid, and *now* it's genuinely symmetric to the IAM grant — because the contributed thing finally is a separable resource. This is the architecturally "right" answer. But: it adds Secrets Manager/SSM as a moving part, needs the task-execution role granted `ssm:GetParameters`, and hinges on `aws_ecs_express_gateway_service` supporting `valueFrom`-style secrets — which is an unverified AWS specific, the same kind of rabbit hole as the task-role question you deliberately deferred. Not a "finish soon" move.

**Escape B — newsetup picks the wiring at scaffold time.** The thing that "adds the env if rds appears" is *newsetup*, not Terraform. Select ecs+rds → emit the live-reference env (today's ecs.tf, one-apply magic). Select ecs alone → emit `var.database_url`. Terraform stays clean in both. Cost: real new complexity in the parts engine (conditional cross-part content) plus two maintained variants. Also not "finish soon."

## My recommendation, given "finish soon" + "I'm coupling them"

You said it yourself: *"I'm coupling them together."* So stop fighting for ecs-standalone. **Make ecs⇒rds the template's contract** — which is *already* exactly what's built: the live reference + `[infra.requires] ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]`. Selecting ecs pulls rds, one apply wires the real endpoint, done. The hardcoded env isn't a wart; it's correct, because in this template ecs never exists without rds.

Then serve "generalist" with **one comment, not machinery** — a couple of commented lines right above that env in ecs/ecs.tf:

Here's the concrete mechanism, traced end to end against the actual engine. The trick that makes it tractable is to **stop the variance from living in `ecs.tf` at all** — collapse it down to a single symbol, then swap only that symbol's definition.

## Step 1: make `ecs.tf` stop varying

Today the variance is buried inside the service resource (the env value), which is unsplittable. So pull it out behind a `local`. `ecs.tf`'s env block becomes stable forever:

```hcl
environment {
  name  = "PROD_DATABASE_URL"
  value = local.database_url     # ← stable. never changes between scenarios.
}
```

Now `ecs.tf` references `local.database_url` and doesn't care where it comes from. All the variance is pushed into the *definition* of that one local — a tiny separate file.

## Step 2: two tiny variant files (one symbol, two definitions)

**Coupled** (the value is the live RDS reference — today's magic):
```hcl
# db_local.when-rds.tf
locals {
  database_url = "postgres://${var.db_username}:${var.db_password}@${aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint}/...?sslmode=require"
}
```

**Standalone** (the value is an input string — generalist):
```hcl
# db_local.unless-rds.tf
variable "database_url" { type = string, default = "" }
locals {
  database_url = var.database_url
}
```

Exactly **one** of these is allowed to land in `./infra/`, ever. If both landed, Terraform errors on duplicate `local.database_url`. So the whole game reduces to: *newsetup must copy the right one and suppress the other.*

## Step 3: the one engine change — presence-gated filenames

newsetup already knows the resolved part set at copy time (the `parts` list in `copy_parts_module`). Teach it one filename rule:

- `foo.when-<part>.tf` → copy **only if** `<part>` ∈ resolved parts, writing it as `foo.tf`.
- `foo.unless-<part>.tf` → copy **only if** `<part>` ∉ resolved parts, writing it as `foo.tf`.

That's the entire new capability: parse a `.when-X` / `.unless-X` infix, check membership, strip the infix on write. In `copy_parts_module`'s file loop, before `shutil.copy2`, a ~6-line gate.

## Step 4: trace both scaffolds

**`--only ecs`** (resolves to `ecs, ecr, iam, _core` — note rds is *not* pulled, because in this model ecs no longer requires it):
- `db_local.when-rds.tf` → rds absent → **skipped**.
- `db_local.unless-rds.tf` → rds absent → copied as `db_local.tf` → `local.database_url = var.database_url`.
- `ecs.tf` references `local.database_url` ✅. No `aws_db_instance` anywhere ✅. Validates standalone. App points wherever you set `database_url` (Supabase, Neon…).

**`--only ecs rds`** (or full infra):
- `db_local.when-rds.tf` → rds present → copied as `db_local.tf` → live reference to `aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint`.
- `db_local.unless-rds.tf` → rds present → **skipped**.
- One `apply`: Terraform sees ecs→rds via the local, builds rds first, injects the real endpoint. The magic, intact.

Never both files → never a duplicate-local error. The "thing that adds the wiring when rds appears" is the filename gate.

## Step 5: the honest wrinkle (tfvars + the variable)

Two satellite pieces also have to ride the gate, or they leak:

- The `variable "database_url"` declaration only makes sense standalone — so it lives **inside** `db_local.unless-rds.tf` (shown above). When rds is present, that file is skipped, so the variable simply doesn't exist. Good.
- The tfvars example line. Standalone wants `database_url = "CHANGE_ME"` in `terraform.tfvars.example`; coupled wants *nothing* (the value is computed, not user-supplied). So the fragment must also be gated: a file named `db.unless-rds.tfvars.fragment`. That means the gate parser has to compose with the existing `*.tfvars.fragment` matcher — strip `.unless-rds`, *then* still recognize `.tfvars.fragment`. Doable, but it's the fiddly bit: two filename conventions now interacting.

## The cost, stated plainly

- **New engine surface:** a filename mini-language (`when-`/`unless-`) that has to compose with the existing fragment-suffix logic. It's small (~10 lines) but it's *permanent vocabulary* every future template author must learn and you must document.
- **Two maintained variants** of the DB wiring that must stay in sync (same env semantics, two definitions).
- **It generalizes**, which is the upside — any "this file only when part X is/ isn't present" need is now expressible (not just DB). That's either a feature or a footgun depending on how much conditional cross-part content you actually expect. So far you have exactly *one* case.

## My call (unchanged, now that you can see the machinery)

Building a general conditional-emission sub-language to serve a single env line is a lot of permanent surface for one case — and it buys you "ecs-standalone," which you said you don't even want ("I'm coupling them"). The same outcome you actually care about (one-apply magic when rds is there) is *already shipping* via the live reference + `requires`. The generalist escape is a one-line manual swap documented in a comment.

So: Escape B is real and clean-ish — the `local.database_url` indirection is genuinely the right shape — but I'd only build the filename-gate engine if a *second or third* conditional-content case shows up. For one line, the comment wins. If you want, I'll do the zero-cost half of this anyway: refactor the env to go through `local.database_url` now (pure cleanup, no engine change), so that *if* you ever want Escape B later, the hard part is already done and it's just dropping the two gated files in.

Plain definitions, in the context of what we were just discussing:

## Variance

**Variance** = the part of something that *changes* between situations, while everything around it stays the same.

In our case: across the two scaffold scenarios (`ecs` alone vs. `ecs + rds`), almost everything in `ecs.tf` is identical. The *only* thing that differs is the database URL value:

- ecs alone → `var.database_url` (a string you type in)
- ecs + rds → `"postgres://...${aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint}..."` (a live reference)

That one differing piece **is the variance**. Everything else is invariant (unchanging). When I said "make `ecs.tf` stop varying," I meant: isolate that one changing piece so the big file stays the same and only a tiny corner changes.

The problem with the *current* layout is that the variance sits **buried inside** the service resource — and Terraform won't let you split a resource across files. So you can't get at just the varying piece. The `local.database_url` trick **extracts the variance** into its own one-line file, so now the only thing that changes between scenarios is which tiny file gets copied.

> Think of it like a power outlet. The wall, the wiring, the room — all invariant. The *plug* you put in is the variance. You don't rebuild the wall to change appliances; you swap the plug. The `local` is the outlet; the two variant files are two plugs.

## Tractable

**Tractable** = manageable, workable, solvable without it blowing up in complexity. (Opposite: *intractable* = practically impossible or unmanageably hard.)

When I said the `local` trick "makes it tractable," I meant: the naive version of Escape B is **intractable** — you'd be trying to conditionally inject a nested block into a resource, which Terraform forbids, so there's no clean way to do it. By extracting the variance to a single symbol, the problem shrinks to "copy one of two tiny files," which *is* manageable — a ~6-line filename rule. The hard problem became an easy one. That's what "made it tractable" means.

So in one sentence: **I isolated the variance (the one thing that changes) to make the problem tractable (small enough to actually solve cleanly).**
